# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity
- [HN] Launch HN: "Launch HN: Expanse (YC P26) – Unlock Wasted GPU Capacity", 2026-06-01, the founders' post and the thread (27 comments), read whole through the HN Algolia API — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48356312 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48356312)
- [WB] expanse.sh as archived 2026-06-01, the day of the Launch HN — https://web.archive.org/web/20260601142950/https://expanse.sh/
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/expanse
- [SITE] expanse.sh, read 2026-10-22 — https://expanse.sh

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Researchers (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work"; the fine-tuning run is the author's.
- Tobias Brandt → [HN] the genomics comment (bursty pipeline, "about 8 different steps", "We need to reserve the $MAX requirements for each").
- Ana Lucía Ferreira → [HN] the student's "so I overestimate" on simulation time; the queue wait for a big request is the author's.
- Kwabena Owusu → author's invention, filling a gap: an ML engineer whose sizes come from past runs on a dashboard, so the problem is not a chorus (against on Importance and Current solution).
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention: a chipped (rather_not_say) story at a quant fund, GUESSED by code.
- Rafael Moreno → author's invention: a vague, habitual story (GUESSED), echoing [HN] "everyone over-requests by two to three times".
- Ingrid Haugen → author's invention: a gate No (writing up, no jobs that week).
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention: a gate No (away at a conference).
- Yusuf Demir → [HN] "snooping on sumbit scripts ... many of them are egregiously bad": a copied script holding eight GPUs.
- Claire Dubois-Martin → author's invention, filling a gap: a licensed binary with no source code, so the tested condition fails ('no').
- Hiroshi Takeda → [HN] "at least for everyone else, I'd would prefer tuning my own usage myself": he profiles a test run (Current solution mostly works; Adoption friction no).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → [HN] "you lose days of work"; the walltime limit and the group allocation are the author's.
- Diego Castañeda → [HN] the student's PDE simulation ("If I'm running a PDE simulation, and I allocate n machines I want to use all of them"); he keeps his margin (Adoption friction probably not).

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

founder.order_why: It moves from naming and market to the context, the window, the problem and its beliefs, the current fix, and then who asks and how, which is the order I'd explain Expanse in.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same kicker and question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'), so the context felt asked twice, with the window on screen 4 splitting it, unless screen 5 is plainly a confirm of what I typed on 3
founder.missing: Nothing asks how big the waste is when a job is over-sized (how many times over-requested, or the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and never used), and that is my core figure (two to three times, 30% to 59%). Nothing touches the cluster operator who actually pays per cluster; the researcher only feels the pain.

PRIMARY.order_why: The flow from failures to what I'd want easier to how guessing went mostly works, but asking how my resource guess went last, after the 'make easier' pick, feels backwards since a bad guess is what caused my mid-run failures, and screens 1 and 2 are both labelled '1 of 4'.
PRIMARY.missing: Why the job failed (out of memory, hit the time limit, preempted), how much work or how many days I lost when it died, and whether I over-request memory, time or GPUs to be safe and then wait longer in the queue.

screens.why4: Voice, text, or let them choose covers it, the three are distinct, and the readiness notes (ready now vs still recording) are exactly what I need to pick 'Read and tap'.
screens.why5: It says 'researchers', my own actor, and nothing of Expanse or the operators leaks into the format choice.
screens.instead: How should researchers answer? — Read and tap (ready now) / AI interviewer Daphne, aloud on video with each question also on screen (ready in a few minutes) / Let them choose when they open the link (ready when Daphne is); name Daphne once and say 'she gets the words right more than 9 times in 10, even somewhere loud'.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how researchers answer, it is obvious I next have to say who gets the link, and nothing here was asked before.
screens.why2: Each option says plainly what I would do (send each their own link, pick a list, or post one link where people already are), and only 'Contacts page' is Keel's own word, which the option explains.
screens.why3: I know who I am reaching: the researchers I can name from our pilots and the HN thread, or a lab Slack or HPC user list I could post to.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list and one open link for a group cover how I would reach researchers on shared clusters, and the three do not overlap.
screens.why5: The screen is about delivery only, my study is untouched, and nothing about Expanse or its roles shows.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is stated with 'Frequency: 4 answered' beside it, but the line names only one of the three short cards and leaves out the 5 needed, so I have to read down to see why 4 decides it.
screens.why_b2: The tally and the Prevalence line ('6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar') are plain, but nothing says why only 4 of the 7 who answered count on the other three cards, so I have to look twice.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are my lines word for word, but Prevalence and Frequency are written as jobs failing mid-run on 3 to 5 days out of 5, when my claim is that everyone over-requests so jobs don't fail and the compute sits idle.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what to do next, not even 'one more answer on each of three cards would call them', and the only footer explains how the verdict is computed.
screens.why_b5: n is visible everywhere, low n is called 'too few' rather than read as a lean, and a pass exactly at 6 of 7 is called 'holding up', not strong.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits directly beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar', so I see both the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 6 for and 1 against over a 0-to-7 axis with the marker at 6, so I can see the count, the n and my bar at a glance.
screens.why_b3: Failing mid-run is in my problem statement, but my prevalence claim was that everyone over-requests by two to three times; this card tests only the under-request side, so I recognise it but it isn't quite the belief I'd put at 8 in 10.
screens.why_b4: The So line just defers to the next two cards; it doesn't say what a common mid-run failure means for a submit-time sizing tool.
screens.why_b5: The card keeps n=7 visible, flags 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and says 'at your bar exactly' rather than calling it strong.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 had a job fail mid-run this week, exactly at your 8-in-10 bar on only 7 people, so it's a lean: failures are common enough to lead your pitch, but check whether they also pad every request, the waste your pilot is priced on.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits beside "4 answered · 5 needed", but the count line says "6 answered · 4 counted", so the header's "answered" contradicts the screen's own count and I have to work out that it means counted.
screens.why_b2: Working days out of 5 and the median of 4 are plain, but "your bar · 3 of 4 (at least 2 in 3)", a ghost cell and a legend split into "at what you said" and "short of it" made me look twice to see that the bar is the share needed and that all four counted are inside my range.
screens.why_b3: My frequency was how often researchers have to guess sizes at submit, 3 to 5 working days out of 5; the card reads it as a job failing mid-run on those days, which is my number and window but a narrower event than the one I set.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic; it doesn't say that all 4 counted fall inside my range and that one more counted answer would settle it.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n visible, says why Mei-Ling and Rafael were not counted and calls the small group "a lean, not a call", so it claims nothing the four answers cannot carry.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of the 6 who answered can be counted and 5 are needed; all 4 had a job fail mid-run on 3 or more of 5 days (middle answer 4), so one more counted researcher would settle it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 counted, 5 needed', but the headline says '4 answered' while the count line says '6 answered · 4 counted', so the deciding number is mislabelled on the same card.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts 8 picks over 4 people, but the bar is given in people (3 of 4) and the strip shows 8 cells (for 3, against 5) as if each were a person, so where I stand needs a second look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Importance and the belief line is word for word the one I checked, with my own five cluster pains as the options.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it should say that one more counted researcher would let Keel call this, and that 3 of 4 already meets my bar.

screens.why_b1: 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, 4 against the 5 needed, and the two agree, so I know it's not called and why.
screens.why_b2: The rows plainly count last-submission outcomes over 4 people with for and against marked, but 'your bar · 3 of 4' puts my count where the bar should be, so I have to work out that the bar is 2 in 3 and I'm already past it.
screens.why_b3: The title and the belief line are exactly the ones I checked: their way of guessing memory, time and GPUs still falls short for most.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it doesn't tell me that one more counted answer settles it, or that the lean so far is my way.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no verdict and why, but the screen never says how the 4 split, so I can't see how close it came to holding or failing.
screens.why_b3: The Importance box carries my belief word for word, and the dimension name is the one I checked.
screens.why_b4: It implies I need more answers, but it doesn't say what Kwabena's reason means for the idea, for example that teams that size jobs from past runs may not feel this pain.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks that I'm the right person, someone who submits jobs to a large shared GPU cluster, before asking anything else.
screens.why2: SLURM, Kubernetes, cluster and GPUs are everyday words in my work, so I can answer straight away.
screens.why3: I know which scheduler I submit to and roughly how many GPUs our shared cluster has, so I can answer without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate, and a gate has no escape, so nothing is missing.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs and says nothing about any product.
screens.why6: One short question with two options is easy to hear once and answer, and SLURM, Kubernetes and GPUs are said the way I say them.

screens.why1: After confirming I run on a big SLURM or Kubernetes cluster, asking whether a job died mid-run in the last week is the obvious next step, since that is the pain I complain about.
screens.why2: 'Job fail mid-run' is how I'd say it myself, and 'the last 5 working days' is clear.
screens.why3: I know exactly which of my jobs got OOM-killed or hit the walltime this week, so I can answer from memory.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete for a gate, but the two escape chips don't fit: a gate shouldn't carry an escape at all, 'I'd rather not say' isn't an allowed escape, and 'I can't recall one particular job submission' doesn't answer a did-a-job-fail question.
screens.why5: The founder's moment is guessing memory, GPUs and time before submitting, but 'fail mid-run' also lets in node crashes and code bugs that have nothing to do with the guess, and the follow-up asks about my 'last job submission' rather than the job that failed.
screens.why6: Spoken as one short question followed by 'Yes or no', which I'd answer at once on hearing it.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did a job of yours get killed for running out of memory or time? Yes; No (no escape).

screens.why1: I just said yes, a job of mine died mid-run this week, so asking how many days it happened is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: 'Fail mid-run' is how I'd say it myself about a job that got OOM-killed or hit its walltime, and the question reads cleanly first time.
screens.why3: I know which days this week I came back to a dead job and a half-finished checkpoint, so I can count them.
screens.why4: One to five covers every possible answer after a yes, with no overlap, and 'I can't recall' fits if the week has blurred.
screens.why5: It stays on jobs not making it to the end, which is the founder's 'run to the end', and nothing about a product or their terms leaks.
screens.why6: It is one short question with 'a number from 1 to 5' and a single escape, so it is easy to hear once and answer.

screens.why1: Right after asking how often a job died mid-run, it makes sense to ask which part of running jobs on the cluster I most want made easier.
screens.why2: Allocation, memory, GPUs and run time are my everyday words; 'last run of jobs' is a little loose, but I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I deal with every one of these myself every week, so I can pick one straight away.
screens.why4: The five are distinct and in my words, but the thing the last two screens were about, a job crashing or getting killed partway and losing the work, has no option, so 'guessing memory, GPUs and run time' has to stand in for it.
screens.why5: The guessing option is one choice among five ordinary cluster pains, and nothing about a product or who is building it shows through.
screens.why6: One short question and five short parallel phrases I can hold, ending with a single escape; it says well.
screens.instead: Think of your last week of jobs on the cluster. Which one would you most like made easier? Getting software working · Moving data on and off · Waiting for a job to start · Guessing memory, GPUs and run time · Jobs dying partway through. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: After asking about jobs dying mid-run, it makes sense to ask how I sized my last submission and how that turned out.
screens.why2: The words are mine (memory, time, GPUs, resubmitted), but the stem says 'job submission' and then 'before submitting a job' again, and each option asks me to match a method and a result at once, so I read it twice.
screens.why3: I size every job myself and I know what happened to my last one, so I can answer this from memory.
screens.why4: Each option ties how I sized it to what happened, so my real case can be missing, like sizing from past runs and still getting OOM-killed, or padding and still hitting the wall-time; 'copied an old script' also overlaps with 'sized from past runs' and gives no outcome.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'memory, GPUs and run time have to be guessed first', and no product or company language reaches me.
screens.why6: There are five options and each is two clauses with a pause in the middle ('padded it a little, it ran, a little idle'), so by the fourth one I can't hold the list in my head.
screens.instead: Think of your last job. How did the memory, time and GPUs you asked for turn out? Options: about right; more than it needed; too little, so it was killed; or I'm not sure what it used. Escape: I can't recall.
